title: Your circle

lines: A RING OF CUSHIONS AND COLD TEA.
cards: A Tuesday evening. A living room with the couch pushed back. A pot of tea going cold because everyone forgot it.

A handful of people on cushions in a rough ring, one mushaf open to a single page, and a question nobody can quite answer: what does this verse actually ask of us on a weekday? Someone checks a commentary.
Someone admits she always misread that line. A teenager asks the question the adults were too shy to ask. No microphone, no stage, no front row.
Just a ring of knees. The halaqah.

teach.b: Halaqah means a circle, and it's what Muslims call a group that sits together to learn. A promise comes attached.

In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that whenever people gather in one of the houses of Allah, reciting His Book and studying it among themselves, calm comes down on them, mercy covers them, angels surround them, and Allah mentions them to those who are with Him.
Notice: not one person reading alone. People studying among themselves. Why a circle and not a lecture?
In a circle everyone faces the middle. The quiet person can be seen. A question can come from anywhere.
The Qur'an, in surah al-Ma'idah, says in Pickthall's words: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty."
A circle is a practical way to help one another: you keep each other coming back, and you hear the parts of a verse you'd have skimmed. What keeps a circle honest?
It can drift into everyone sharing opinions with nothing underneath. So a circle does well to keep one anchor: a teacher who visits, a trusted commentary, a book worked through page by page.

teach.h: AN ANCHOR, AND I DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: And good manners: one person speaks at a time, nobody mocks a question, and anyone may say, I don't know. Saying it out loud, in front of friends, is part of learning together.

how: Muslims gather in a halaqah, a study circle, at a mosque or in a home, to read a passage of the Qur'an or a hadith together, often with a teacher or a trusted commentary, and to discuss what it asks of daily life.

o: a lecture given from a stage to a large crowd
a ring of worshippers circling the Kaaba
a circle of people who sit facing each other to learn

p: a circle that sits to learn
the hadith's promise to the circle

s: a halaqah is a lecture from a stage
a halaqah is a circle where everyone faces the middle and a question can come from anywhere.
in a hadith, people studying the Book together are surrounded by angels
Sahih Muslim: calm comes down on them, mercy covers them, angels surround them.

games.q: your new circle has met three times. it's turning into everyone sharing opinions about a verse with nothing underneath them. what helps?
o: add an anchor: a visiting teacher or a trusted commentary.
games.why: a circle does well to keep one anchor, a teacher, a commentary or a book worked through page by page, and the manners to let anyone say I don't know.

practice: In your mind, draw a small ring and seat a few people you'd actually like to learn with, a friend, a cousin, a neighbor, not the most impressive ones but the ones who'd show up.

Place one thing in the middle, a short surah, a single hadith, a chapter of a book, and notice how it feels to imagine not learning alone. If you pray, ask Allah in your own words to bless whatever circle you join.

wordCard.voice: Halaqah. A circle of people who sit facing one another to learn their faith together. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a circle; a study circle.

carryVoice: Your line: learn together. Nobody in the ring has to know it all. That's today, done.
